scenarios.title: The Boomer Bastion
scenarios.briefing: It is day one of WW3. Several NATO assets have been held back from other combat duties with the specific purpose of attacking the Soviet boomers at home in their bastion. Additionally, the SOSUS line must be manned to protect a passing convoy.
scenarios.victoryConditions: NATO win the game by sinking an SSBN payload value of 8. The Soviet player may reduce the current Payload value back by one for each Soviet submarine step that makes it over the SOSUS line (remove it from the game). The minimum resulting total is zero (it cannot be negative). NATO may add one Payload point each by damaging or sinking the Kiev.
scenarios.specialRules: The Bastion cannot have Bad Weather (ignore any such results) but otherwise generate weather for East and North. The game lasts for three turns. No cards are used in this scenario. Optionally, both players can draw five cards at the start of the game and use only Reaction Events - ignore the rest of the card.
scenarios.opsTrackNote: Use the Small Scenario OPS Track.

alterations.title: Scenario 1a: Yankee Hunting
alterations.description:
Setup as Scenario #1 and add the following units.

Scenario Alterations:
- One Yankee step must be killed for NATO to win the game.
- NATO may add a Payload value point at the end of each turn if any Yankee is more than 1 zone from a First Strike zone.
- The Soviet units starting the game over the SOSUS line cannot reduce the current Payload value sunk by crossing over the SOSUS line - the scenario special rule is ignored for them.
- NATO OPS increase to 7. Generate weather for Mid and West zones as well (everything except the Mediterranean).

scenarios.coachNotes:
## Strategic shape

This scenario is the game's set-piece submarine duel: NATO has three turns to sink 8 Payload value of Soviet SSBNs huddled inside the Bastion (2.3.4), while the Soviet player races to break attack subs out across the GIUK SOSUS line (2.3.6) to chip that total back down. With 5 NATO OPS and 7 Soviet OPS per turn and no card-based events in play, the entire scenario is a brawl decided by which sub force gets its dice when it matters.

## NATO priorities

Get NATO sub groups under the Arctic ice on turn 1 so they can drop into the Bastion turn 2 with a free move and no surface ASW to fear. The Sturgeon and Los Angeles attack subs are the win condition; they have Defense 10 and saves, which is how NATO survives the Bastion's lethal natural-1 rule (2.3.4) and Hydrophone Reaction (2.3.6). Keep UK MP units on patrol over the GIUK Gap so they intercept any Soviet sub the Soviet player tries to slip across the SOSUS line, denying the Soviet Payload reduction. Save the Norwegian diesels for blocking, not heroics, they will lose every duel with an Alpha or Bear-F.

## Soviet priorities

Form the Kiev Task Force on turn 1 and sail it to the Bastion to add 2 ASW dice plus the Bastion bonus to the defense. Keep SSNs and noisy escorts in the Bastion in pairs so escorts absorb the hits intended for SSBNs (the escort's only job is to take the bullet, see Capital Ships hits allocation). Save 1 to 2 OPS each turn to run a sub or two across the SOSUS line, every step that escapes claws a Payload point back. Note Bastion weather is ignored (scenario rule), which keeps Bear-F maritime patrol effective every turn.

## Decision points

Turn 2 is the hinge. NATO must commit subs into the Bastion that turn or run out of clock; the entry turn triggers Hydrophone Reaction (2.3.6) and any natural 1 on later ASW rolls in the Bastion takes a step from the attacker (2.3.4). The Soviet player decides whether to sortie Deltas or fight purely defensively; sortied SSBNs that cross the SOSUS line reduce the kill count (special rule), but exposed Deltas with Defense 8 are easy NATO kills.

## Pitfalls

NATO commonly under-screens with MP and lets Soviet attack subs cross SOSUS unopposed, gifting back Payload. NATO also overcommits all subs at once and gets shredded by Soviet ASW on entry. The Soviet player commonly forgets escort doctrine and lets SSBN steps absorb hits that a Victor or noisier sub should have taken. Both sides forget the Kiev itself is worth a Payload point if damaged or sunk per the scenario victory rule.

scenarios.title: Ace Mobile & First Convoys
scenarios.briefing: D+2. While the fight rages underwater in the North, NATO sorties convoys to sea heading for the French ports. Meanwhile ACE Mobile - NATO's rapid reaction force, sets off from the UK to Trondheim. The Soviets have earmarked two regiments of naval aviation and 18 submarines to interdict these forces.
scenarios.victoryConditions: The Soviet player wins if both the Convoy and the Amphib take three hits, otherwise NATO wins so long as the Amphib makes it to Trondheim and the Convoy to a French port.
scenarios.specialRules: Prior to beginning play NATO may move any two Air Units and put them On Patrol. The British may deploy their Surface Units in up to 2 different Task Forces as desired, beginning in British ports but formed up so there is no further OPS cost to sail them. Play continues for a maximum of 4 turns. The Soviet player has one spy available, after every use remove it from the game on a roll of 1-4. When a Convoy/Amphib reaches port remove the entire Task Force from the scenario. No cards are used in this scenario. Optionally, both players can draw five cards at the start of the game and use only Reaction Events - ignore the rest of the card. UK Air Units cannot enter the North 9-10 zone in this scenario.
scenarios.opsTrackNote: Use the Small Scenario OPS Track.

alterations.title: Scenario 2a: Extended
alterations.description:
Setup as Scenario #2 and add the following units.

Scenario Alterations: The Soviets must hit all three targets (Convoys & Amphib) for three hits apiece or six hits on any two to win the game. Soviets receive 9 OPS per turn.

scenarios.coachNotes:
## Strategic shape

This is the textbook convoy interdiction scenario: NATO must shepherd one Convoy to a French port and the ACE Mobile Amphib to Trondheim across four turns, while a Soviet force of 18 submarines plus two regiments of naval aviation tries to put three hits each on both targets. Soviet wins if both targets eat three hits, NATO wins on any other outcome. With 6 NATO OPS and 8 Soviet OPS per turn and no cards in play, this is a hide-and-seek game decided by detection and air strike economy.

## NATO priorities

Use the free pre-game move to put two Air Units on patrol covering the Mid Atlantic and North Sea approaches. The British may pre-form their surface ships into up to two Task Forces with no OPS cost, so build one strong escort around the Convoy and another around the Amphib. The Amphib has the harder run because UK Air Units cannot enter North 9 to 10 (scenario rule), so it transits without UK MP cover until it crosses south. Spend OPS aggressively on ASW (7.2) against detected Soviet subs in the Convoy's path; do not let a Foxtrot or Tango sit in a chokepoint zone unmolested.

## Soviet priorities

The Soviet player owns one spy (removed on a roll of 1 to 4 after each use, scenario rule), so save it for the moment a Convoy or Amphib needs a Poor detection upgraded to Good for a coordinated missile shot. Spread submarines along the convoy lanes rather than clustering: a sub on patrol (5.2.3) in West 4 or North 3 to 4 can intercept the convoy track without spending OPS to move. Pre-stage Backfires and Badgers at Kola with tanker support; a coordinated air strike on a detected Task Force is the fastest way to put three hits on the Amphib. Note the errata: the listed tanker is actually a Tu-16 Strike, so you have one tanker, one Tu-22 and two Tu-16.

## Decision points

The most important call is whether to route the Convoy and Amphib together or split them. Together gives one strong AAW and ASW bubble but one detected target absorbs everything; split halves the Soviet target density but doubles his shots per turn. The Soviet player must decide early whether to commit Backfires to one big strike against the Convoy or husband them for two smaller strikes; the first option risks losing the strike to F-14 CAP, the second risks running out of turns.

## Pitfalls

NATO commonly forgets that a delivered Task Force removes from the scenario (special rule); landing the Amphib early at Trondheim retires its escorts too and weakens the late game. Both sides forget that bad weather in the destination zone of a Hydrophone Barrier blocks ASW reaction (2.3.6), which matters when subs transit the English Channel. NATO should also not idle Air Units defensively; an MP that never goes searching is wasted OPS.

scenarios.title: Kirov's & Carriers
scenarios.briefing: It is day five of WW3. Both Icelandic and English airbases have been subjected to repeated attack by Badger bombers and are inoperable. Communications intercepts have detected a Soviet amphibious force forming in Severomorsk. Satellite recon confirms the force is no longer in port as of 8 hours ago. Intelligence expects a landing in the area of Trondheim, Norway. Two carrier groups are in the area and are the only force standing between the Bad Banner Fleet and Oslo.
scenarios.victoryConditions: NATO wins the game by preventing any Troops markers being placed through an Amphibious Landing at Trondheim. The Soviet player wins if any troops have landed.
scenarios.specialRules:
Use the Small Scenario OPS Track for this game. NATO 9 OPS, Soviet 10 OPS.

Prior to beginning game roll one die for each of Keflavik and the Scottish airbases; place heavy damage on an 8,9 or 10 otherwise place light damage. Place the number of die rolled to cause that level of damage (e.g. place 3 dice on UK Airbase if heavily damaged or 1 hit if lightly damaged) The Soviets may deploy their Surface Units in up to 3 different Task Forces as desired and may use nuclear submarines in North 9-10 as part of a Task Force.

Play continues for a maximum of 4 turns.

No cards are used in this scenario. Optionally, both players can draw five cards at the start of the game and use only Reaction Events - ignore the rest of the card.
scenarios.opsTrackNote: Use the Small Scenario OPS Track.

alterations.title: The Days Before
alterations.description: Start with the Soviet ships all in port, and the US carrier Task Forces both 2 zones West of their parallel-at-start positions. This allows the fight to develop, rather than being a knife fight in a phone booth.

scenarios.coachNotes:
## Strategic shape

This is the surface combat scenario the game is named for: a Soviet amphibious task force is steaming for Trondheim with Kirov-class escorts, and two US carrier groups are the only force that can stop it. NATO wins by preventing any Soviet troops landing at Trondheim; Soviet wins the moment one Troops marker hits the Invasion Track (8.1.1). With 9 NATO OPS, 10 Soviet OPS, four turns and no cards in play, this is a missile-and-detection brawl between heavy surface forces.

## NATO priorities

Keflavik and the Scottish airbases roll for setup damage; expect at least light damage and plan as though land-based air over North 7 to 10 is degraded. The two carrier groups are the only reliable hammer, so coordinate strikes (5.3.5) by putting both carriers in the same Sea Zone for one big strike rather than two weak ones. Use F-14 CAP and intrinsic MP (6.1.2.2) to detect the Soviet TF early; once detected, US CAGs can SEAD and salvo missiles. Prioritize sinking the Amphibs before they reach the Trondheim landing zone, not the escorts; one undamaged Amphib lands two troops (8.1.1 hits table) and ends the game.

## Soviet priorities

The Soviets may deploy in up to three Task Forces and may include nuclear submarines in North 9 to 10 as part of a TF (special rule). Use this to build one strong screen group with Kirov and Slava to absorb US missile fire, a second containing the Amphibs to hide behind it, and a third sub-led TF to threaten the carriers. Sail under the bad weather front when possible; bad weather slows movement but it also halves NATO ASW and detection rolls. The Amphib only needs to reach the Trondheim zone and place a Landing marker (5.1.3.2), which then resolves on the next chance to move; planning around that two-turn process is mandatory.

## Decision points

The scenario turns on whether the US closes to missile range or keeps the carriers back. Closing means a US first strike with Tomahawks and CAGs; staying back means trying to win with air strikes alone, which is much harder against a Kirov-grade SAM screen. The Soviet decision is whether to try and sink a US carrier first or punch through with the Amphibs. Sinking a carrier earns 2 NATO loss points (3.5.1) plus one more if it happens north of the SOSUS line, but spending three turns hunting it lets the four-turn clock run out.

## Pitfalls

The Soviet player commonly tries to land turn 1, which is impossible (the Landing marker takes a turn to resolve per 5.1.3.2, then the landing resolves the next chance to move). NATO commonly throws CAGs at the Kirov screen and gets ground down by SS-N-19 Shipwreck salvoes (7.4.2.4); strike the Amphib in the same zone instead since it has no real SAMs. Both sides forget intrinsic MP only rolls during Ships events (6.1.2.2), not on demand.

scenarios.title: Attack on the Kola Peninsula
scenarios.briefing: It is day two of WWIII. The United States Navy has decided to strike the Soviet Kola Peninsula bases in order to halt the threat from Soviet naval aviation. Four aircraft carriers are currently 1500 nautical miles from their targets and steaming at high speed to the Northeast. The Soviets have two full divisions of strike aircraft, two divisions of fighters and the most formidable air defense system on the planet.
scenarios.victoryConditions: NATO wins the game by heavily damaging both the Kola Peninsula airbase and port facilities, otherwise the Soviets win. Casualties on either side are irrelevant.
scenarios.specialRules: Play continues for a maximum of 5 turns. Set up the Soviets first and then NATO. There are no NATO onsite missiles in the scenario as it takes place in 1983. No cards are used in this scenario. Optionally, both players can draw five cards at the start of the game and use only Reaction Events - ignore the rest of the card.
scenarios.opsTrackNote: Use the Small Scenario OPS Track.

alterations.title: #1 Use Nuclear Weapons
alterations.description: Try the scenario with nuclear weapons at sea in effect. This forces Soviet naval air power as the Americans have no corresponding weapon to use against them, and nuclear bombardment of Kola itself would all but guarantee a response against a significant American or British strategic target. To balance the increased firepower, allow the US player to take any two of the following cards: SAM Trap, Special Forces, Fighter Recovery, Economic Control, Radar Decoys.

alterations.title: #2 Cruise Missiles
alterations.description: Play the scenario in 1985 allowing the US to use cruise missiles and adding US-6 to the US forces. The Soviet player may place an additional RORSAT in any zone of the map.

alterations.title: #3 All the Toys
alterations.description: Add 2 Ticonderoga VLS to the US forces, and add a Bear-G at Kola to the Soviet setup, the Victor-III (I) and the Akula anywhere in a North Sea Zone (placed last, after everything else is on the map).

scenarios.coachNotes:
## Strategic shape

This is a five-turn carrier strike race against the world's heaviest land-based air defense. NATO must heavily damage both the Kola airbase and the Kola port (7.5.4) to win; the Soviet player wins by holding. Casualties are irrelevant, only Kola damage counts. With 10 OPS per side and four US carriers in play, NATO has firepower but every Kola hit hands the Soviet player a First Strike Point (7.5.4), so even a winning damage race can fuel a Soviet nuclear reply if optional rules are in use.

## NATO priorities

Close to N7 to 8 carrier strike range fast, then strike in waves: SEAD with two CAGs together gets a bonus SEAD die (7.5.1.1), so always stack two carriers per strike to suppress the Soviet SAMs. Each US CAG attacking Kola may split bombing between airfield and port targets in the same zone (7.5.1.3). The 1983 setup has no NATO onsite missiles (special rule), so Tomahawk is off the table unless playing the 1985 alteration. Husband F-14 escorts for the Backfire and Badger waves that will hit on turns 2 and 3; without F-14 CAP a single Soviet strike can mission-kill a carrier (3.5.1).

## Soviet priorities

Setup goes Soviets first, then NATO (special rule), so the Soviet player must commit SAM and fighter posture without knowing where the carrier groups will lurk. Concentrate Su-27 and MiG-31 CAP in Kola and use Bear and Badger as long-range strike to attrit the carriers; one carrier sunk north of the SOSUS line is worth 3 NATO loss points (3.5.1) which can effectively replace the win condition with a Soviet political victory in a campaign mindset, but here it just bleeds NATO's strike capability. Bombing the carriers is the only way to slow the damage clock since stopping bombs once they reach Kola is hard.

## Decision points

The scenario turns on whether NATO splits between airbase and port or pounds one to heavy damage first. Splitting risks ending with two lightly-damaged facilities and a loss; concentrating means one facility eats every Soviet SAM die. The Soviet decision is whether to fly Backfires out on turn 1 or wait until the carriers are detected; a wasted strike against an undetected Task Force is a giveaway, but late commitment lets US CAGs hit Kola twice before the Backfires can answer.

## Pitfalls

NATO commonly forgets that each hit on Kola gives the Soviet a First Strike Point (7.5.4); if playing with nuclear weapons at sea (optional Use Nuclear Weapons alteration), winning the bombing race can lose the campaign by trigger. The Soviet player commonly leaves SAMs unsuppressed; the SEAD step (7.5.1.1) reduces SAM values for the rest of the attack and a coordinated SEAD die from two CAGs can gut the defense before the bombing roll. Both sides forget the +1 SAM DRM if the Soviet has the SAM Technology marker (7.5.1.2), which makes optional Soviet tech selection meaningful.

scenarios.title: Baltic Bust-Up
scenarios.briefing: It is day one of WWI3. The Politburo has instructed Soviet commanders to take Denmark as a priority. Badger regiments have been allocated to destroy the German airbases, and submarines will secure the Baltic Sea. Meanwhile, NATO forces are ready and waiting to defend their Danish allies.
scenarios.victoryConditions: The Soviets win the game by landing 2 Troops markers in Denmark, otherwise NATO wins. Casualties on either side are irrelevant.
scenarios.specialRules: Play continues for a maximum of 4 turns. Instead of the usual weather process roll a single die each turn - the Baltic experiences Bad Weather on a '10' and must have clear weather the following turn (do not roll, it's automatically clear the turn after). Remember to resolve the amphibious invasion landing procedure each time the Soviet player tries to land. No cards are used in this scenario. Optionally, both players can draw five cards at the start of the game and use only Reaction Events - ignore the rest of the card.
scenarios.opsTrackNote: Use the Small Scenario OPS Track.
scenarios.coachNotes:
## Strategic shape

This is a four-turn amphibious assault on Denmark. The Soviets need to land two Troops markers in Denmark via Amphibious Landing (8.1.1) to win; anything less is a NATO victory. With 6 OPS per side, this is the most surface-and-air dependent scenario in the book; the Baltic constrains options and the special weather rule (a single die per turn, with a 10 forcing automatic clear weather the following turn) creates timing windows neither side can fully predict.

## NATO priorities

Get German Tornado strike squadrons over the Baltic on day one. The Soviet has only one path: through North 1 to 2 and out, and German STK from Schleswig and Kiel can reach the landing zones (CL#11 puts Denmark interceptor level at 3). Spend OPS on Air Strike against the Soviet TF in port before it sails; once at sea with mines cleared the Soviet has 6 dice for landings turn 1 to 2 (8.1.1). NATO surface and submarine assets in the Baltic can fire white and blue missiles without a card (special exception per 7.4.1.2), so use that one-time advantage to ambush the Amphib TF before it reaches a landing site.

## Soviet priorities

The landing is the only path to victory, so every OPS not spent escorting the Amphib TF is wasted. Badger regiments are allocated to destroy German airbases; hit Kiel and Schleswig on turn 1 to suppress German STK before they can hit the landing zone. Submarines secure the Baltic Sea: place them in North 1 to 2 to keep NATO Task Forces from interrupting the landing approach. On the landing roll itself, cancel the most lethal dice with missiles per 8.1.1: a 4 to 5 result is Ships hits cancelled by two black or yellow missiles, a 6 to 8 is Air strike hits cancelled by four SAMs not counted twice.

## Decision points

The scenario turns on the bad weather die. A 10 on turn 1 forces clear weather turn 2, which makes turn 2 a great landing window for the Soviet but also great strike weather for the German Tornados. The Soviet must decide whether to push for a turn 2 landing (4 dice per 8.1.1, easier to land troops) or wait until turn 3 (3 dice, harder). NATO must decide whether to commit Tornado strikes to Soviet airbases first to stop the Badger attrition or directly to the Amphib TF.

## Pitfalls

The Soviet commonly forgets to resolve the amphibious landing procedure each landing attempt (special rule reminder); skipping it gives free troops with no defensive roll. NATO commonly forgets that German STK is lethal against the Soviet Amphibs but very fragile if the airbases get hit, so protecting Kiel and Schleswig with CAP is paramount. The scenario is widely considered pro-NATO on dice alone; if it feels lopsided, common adjustments are giving NATO +1 OPS or starting hits on Soviet Amphibs, but those are house rules not part of the printed scenario.

scenarios.title: Campaign Game
scenarios.briefing: This is the full game, with three possible starting years: 1983, 1985 and 1989 and three possible start types - strategic surprise, tactical surprise and extended build-up. The 'standard' game is the tactical surprise scenario which postulates an approximate 1 month of warning time for NATO to prepare for the impending Soviet attack. For your first campaign game, try 1983 - tactical scenario, no 'options' in play.
scenarios.victoryConditions:
Victory is determined by the start type chosen (Strategic Surprise, Tactical Surprise, or Build-up). See the special rules for each start type.

See also (3.5) for Determining Victory and (3.5.1) for NATO Losses tracking.
scenarios.specialRules:
Setup the game based on the scenario and your selected and then follow this checklist to start the game.

Both players draw 5 cards each and inspect them.

Note: Any markers not mentioned are put in easy reach and if a numeric marker starts at 0 (there is no zero box).

startTypes.label: Strategic Surprise
startTypes.specialRules:
All Convoys begin with two hits during setup and Turns 1 and 2. During Turns 3 through 5 this is reduced to one hit. From Turn 6, Convoys form normally with no hits.

This represents the lack of pre-war time to properly form-up NATO shipping, meaning that convoys have less ships for the first two weeks of the war.

startTypes.label: Tactical Surprise
startTypes.specialRules: There are no special rules in play here.

startTypes.label: Extended Build-up
startTypes.specialRules:
The Soviet player takes 2 First Strike Points at the start of the game. NATO places two Convoys on Turns 1, 3, 5, 7 and 9 (all odd Convoy turns) - note that if NATO is unlucky with weather it is possible there are not enough Convoys to place. If this happens, the missing Convoys are received as soon as they are available.

NATO has a huge number of convoy ships available, having formed up the merchant navies of Europe to support the war effort. The Soviets are more prepared to use reserves or nuclear weapons, and have significant force at-sea.

startTypeScaling.label: Breakdown choice - NATO may place 1 US Sturgeon and or 1 US Los Angeles sub into the Destroyed box to take the two matching breakdown counters, placed where either sub(s) were or with any at-sea Task Force lacking a submarine counter. Similarly NATO may place these surface ships US 4-6 in the Destroyed box, take the US 13-17 in-port hits replace each removed unit with one or two replacement ships. Any not placed may begin in the USA.
ship units may be moved to any other NATO base(s) or Task Forces at sea
One NATO Task Force may be formed up and placed within 2 Sea Zones of its origin port forces from that port. (UK and FR ports count as the same origin port for this purpose).
Submarine Units can be placed anywhere on the map
Air Units can be placed within their range 'On Patrol' - either MP air or fighters
The at-sea carriers beginning the game in TF Hammer may be relocated to new or existing Task Forces anywhere except the Mediterranean, and not North of the GIUK Gap.
Optional: Draw 2 'options' markers from a cup and select one to keep. Repeat for each First Strike Point given to the Soviet player (maximum of 2 picks).
The Soviet player may purchase Soviet Technology markers. Reduce the Spies Track by the number on each marker put into play.

The Soviet player may take one Tu-22 from the destroyed box (if present) by removing 2 Tu-16 Badgers or the Tu-95 Bear-G. Place it on the Kola, Baltic, Black Sea or Syrian bases. (Trading assets with the Far East)
Move up to three strike Air Units to any Soviet bases. (except for Cuba)
Move up to three Surface Units to any Soviet bases. (except for Cuba)
subs can be placed anywhere on the map
additional subs may be placed within two Sea Zones of a Soviet base (except for Cuba)

Soviet Task Force(s) may be created from any units originating in a single Soviet port (per TF) and placed on the map anywhere marked with a Poor detection. If placed within one zone of a NATO TF, instead mark with a Good detection.
Roll weather for all zones. If weather is placed in a zone with a Task Force, place a 'Moved' marker on it (the Task Force has been within the Bad Weather for some time and will have soon).
Battletales: Roll detection on all NATO Task Forces at sea with one die. The Soviet player may choose any one Task Force (two in the build-up scenario) and use two dice instead
Begin the game starting with the Convoy Placement Phase.
Optional: Draw 2 'options' markers from a cup and select one to keep. Repeat for each First Strike Point discarded or spy expended (maximum of 2 given).

scenarios.coachNotes:
## Strategic shape

The full game runs 12 turns and lives or dies on the convoy lane and the Soviet land advance. The Soviets need four Hammer and Sickle icons on overrun locations (3.5); NATO wins by preventing that, with NATO Losses (3.5.1) giving the Soviets a free Hammer and Sickle if it hits 6. Three start types change the opening posture: Strategic Surprise gives Convoys starting hits, Tactical Surprise is the balanced default, Extended Build-up gives Soviets 2 First Strike Points and NATO double-convoys on odd turns.

## NATO priorities

Convoys are the war. Each Convoy with up to 2 hits cancels a Soviet War Track advance (3.5); two Partial Supply Convoys (3 to 4 hits) combine to do the same. Form one strong carrier TF in the Mid Atlantic to anchor convoy defense, keep another carrier free to respond to Soviet sorties. Use F-14 escorts to protect MP doing the searching (6.1.2.1); without detection there is no ASW. The 1983 tactical surprise setup is the recommended first play; Extended Build-up gives a wider canvas but the Soviet 2 FSP head start can lead to early nuclear pressure.

## Soviet priorities

Backfire and Badger strikes plus submarine attrition are the offensive weight (7.4); the surface fleet cannot win alone. Get the Bastion stable in setup with 6 SSN escorts and several diesels; the Bastion's defenses (2.3.4) plus a Bear-F screen do most of the work, freeing offensive air for convoy interdiction. Decide early whether to sortie SSBNs to First Strike zones (2.3.5) for FSP generation and accept NATO ASW risk, or keep them in the Bastion and earn FSPs only via Second Strike cards. Battlefield nuclear weapons cost 5 FSP (9.1) and convert a 2-Hammer space to 1.

## Decision points

Setup dominates the early game. The NATO setup steps reshuffle the deck before any dice roll: pre-forming a Task Force within 2 zones of port lets a carrier deploy without spending opening OPS; placing subs anywhere on the map means choosing between Bastion ambush positions and SOSUS lane patrols. The Soviet Battletales step (rolling detection on NATO TFs at start) decides the opening fight; a Good detection on the Hammer carrier opens a Backfire shot turn 1.

## Pitfalls

Both sides commonly try the campaign without first running the small scenarios; this rewards system mastery and punishes rules lookups across 12 turns. Soviets commonly chase FSP generation without watching the Soviet Stability Track (9.4); every SSBN killed rolls stability dice on the Soviet Nuclear Strike Capability Track (9.1.2), and a coup ends the game immediately. NATO commonly underweights mine clearance and port repair; one Heavy mined French port adds 2 hits per Convoy (5.1.4), which turns Full Convoys into Partial or worse over the campaign.
